comments.text: Very interesting. Though I suspect there will be a need to grade quality of the micro services to avoid hussles and scams. Let's use the example of weather forecast. Norway gives their basic world forecasts out for free, someone makes an agent that connects to it and sell the results as premium weather forecasts for the bahamas. How could the buying agent know it was sold the quality required? Or someone could make an agent that buys premium data from a weather service, but only once per day (and then reselling that data multiple times in that day at a tiny bit cheaper than the real weather service). The  hussle would be hard to detect, and could easily be dangerous when the real weather turn, the weather services updates, but the intermediate (and cheaper) husselers don't actually update their data before a day has passed.

comments.author: @jwolpert
comments.text: Blockchain is not necessary for this, nor is it a way to handle the speed needed by AI agents. Quite the opposite. Blockchain transactions are slower and handle less throughput. Traditional compute is perfectly capable of handling the commerce. What makes blockchain — seem — like it is faster is regulatory arbitrage. Take away regulatory requirements that involve human checks, and traditional systems are faster and better than blockchain by orders of magnitude. Microtransactions are especially bad for blockchain. There is a marginal cost to every blockchain transaction. Traditional systems have capital costs that amortize over use, driving marginal costs to limit-zero.  Blockchains require fees to cover the miners or validators in a decentralized regime to process the transaction.  This is a terrible idea for micropayments.  Those of us who have actually worked on blockchains get this — though some of us still get paid a lot of money to not mention what we know.
